LECTURER: In this lecture, we'll look at how migratory birds find their way across thousands of kilometres, often returning to exactly the same nesting site each year.
To appreciate the scale of the challenge, consider the Arctic tern. It breeds in the Arctic and spends the northern winter near Antarctica, so each year it travels between the polar regions. Tracking studies have shown that, because it follows winding routes to take advantage of winds, a single bird may fly more than seventy thousand kilometres in a year.
How do birds navigate? Research suggests they use several systems, often in combination, rather than relying on a single cue.
The first is the sun. Birds can use the sun's position as a compass. But because the sun moves across the sky during the day, this requires an internal clock to compensate. Experiments in which birds' body clocks were shifted by keeping them under artificial light confirmed this: their sense of direction shifted by a predictable amount.
The second is the stars. Many songbirds migrate at night. In a famous series of experiments, birds were placed in a planetarium. When the artificial night sky was rotated, the birds changed the direction they tried to fly. It seems young birds learn the point around which the stars rotate, which indicates north.
The third cue, and perhaps the most intriguing, is the Earth's magnetic field. Birds appear to detect both the direction of the field and its angle relative to the ground, which varies with latitude. Exactly how they sense it is still being investigated. One leading theory involves special molecules in the eye, meaning that birds may actually see the magnetic field in some way.
Closer to their destination, birds also rely on landmarks such as coastlines, rivers and mountain ranges. And some species, especially seabirds, appear to use smell to locate their colonies.
A key finding is the difference between young and experienced birds. In one classic experiment, starlings were captured during migration and transported several hundred kilometres to the side of their usual route. The adults corrected their course and reached the normal wintering area. The young birds, however, continued flying in their original direction, ending up somewhere entirely new. This suggests that young birds inherit a compass direction, but the ability to navigate to a specific location must be learned.

• Sun compass: needs an internal (2) ______
• Stars: tested in a (3) ______
• Magnetic field: may be detected by molecules in the (4) ______
• Experiment with (5) ______: only adults corrected course after being moved

LECTURER: Today's lecture addresses a long-running debate in linguistics: is there a critical period for language acquisition — an age after which it becomes much harder, or even impossible, to learn a language fully?
The idea was popularised in the 1960s by the neurologist Eric Lenneberg. He argued that the brain is especially flexible in childhood and that this window closes around puberty. Evidence for this came partly from studies of patients recovering from brain injuries. Children who suffered damage to the language areas of the brain often recovered their language abilities remarkably well, whereas adults with similar injuries typically did not.
The strongest evidence for a critical period in first-language acquisition comes from rare and tragic cases of children who were isolated and received almost no exposure to language until later in childhood. These children, once rescued, could learn many words, but they generally struggled to master grammar. However, such cases are difficult to interpret, because these children also experienced severe neglect, which may have affected development in many ways.
More systematic evidence comes from deaf individuals who were first exposed to sign language at different ages. Studies have found that those who learned sign language from birth used its grammar more accurately than those who started in adolescence, even after decades of use.
What about second languages? Here the picture is more complex. One aspect where age seems to matter clearly is pronunciation. People who begin learning a language after early childhood rarely achieve a native-like accent. For grammar, the evidence is more mixed. A large online study in 2018, involving over half a million participants, suggested that the ability to learn grammar remains strong until around the age of seventeen or eighteen, and then gradually declines.
But it's important to note what age doesn't determine. Adults often learn faster than children in the early stages, because they can use explicit strategies, draw on their first language, and understand grammatical explanations. Children's advantage appears mainly in the eventual level they reach, given many years of immersion.
Many researchers now prefer the term "sensitive period" rather than "critical period", because the decline seems gradual rather than sudden, and individual variation is large. Motivation, quality of input and amount of exposure all play major roles, which is encouraging news for adult learners.

[Notes]
Critical period hypothesis

• Isolated children: learned words but not (2) ______
• Deaf people who learned sign language from birth more accurate
• Second languages: age clearly affects (3) ______
• 2018 study: grammar ability strong until about 17–18
• Adults learn faster at first: use (4) ______ strategies
• Many researchers prefer the term (5) ______ period

LECTURER: Good morning. In this lecture, I'll explain what causes the tides, and why their size changes over the course of a month.
Most coastlines experience two high tides and two low tides roughly every day. More precisely, the cycle repeats about every twenty-four hours and fifty minutes, which is why high tide is a little later each day. That extra fifty minutes is a clue to the cause, because it matches the time it takes the Moon to return to the same position in the sky.
The main driver of the tides is the Moon's gravity. The Moon pulls on the whole Earth, but the pull is slightly stronger on the side facing the Moon and slightly weaker on the far side. On the near side, the ocean is pulled towards the Moon, creating a bulge of water. On the far side, another bulge forms, because the solid Earth is pulled towards the Moon more strongly than the water there. So there are two bulges, and as the Earth rotates, a given coastline passes through both of them, giving two high tides.
The Sun also affects tides, but its influence is less than half that of the Moon. Although the Sun is enormously more massive, it's also much further away, and tidal effects decrease very rapidly with distance.
The interaction between the Sun and Moon explains the monthly variation. When the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line, which happens at new moon and full moon, their effects combine. This produces spring tides, with very high high tides and very low low tides. Note that the name has nothing to do with the season; it comes from the idea of the water springing up. When the Sun and Moon are at right angles to each other, at the quarter moons, their effects partly cancel out, giving neap tides, where the difference between high and low water is small.
Local geography has a huge effect too. In the open ocean, the tidal range is often less than a metre. But in some bays and estuaries, the shape of the coastline funnels the water and amplifies the tide. The Bay of Fundy in Canada has the largest tidal range in the world, up to around sixteen metres. Other places, such as much of the Mediterranean, have very small tides.

• Neap tides: Sun and Moon at right angles
• Tidal range increased by the shape of bays and (5) ______

LECTURER: Today we're looking at microplastics, an environmental issue that has received enormous attention over the last decade.
Microplastics are usually defined as pieces of plastic smaller than five millimetres. Researchers divide them into two categories. Primary microplastics are manufactured at that small size. Secondary microplastics form when larger plastic items, such as bottles, bags and fishing nets, break down over time, mainly through exposure to sunlight and the action of waves.
Where do most microplastics come from? The answer surprises many people. Some of the largest sources are not obvious plastic litter at all. One is synthetic clothing. Materials like polyester and nylon release tiny fibres every time they're washed. A single wash load can release hundreds of thousands of fibres, many of which pass through water treatment plants and into rivers and the sea.
Another major source is vehicle tyres. As tyres wear down on roads, they shed small particles, which are washed into drains by rain or carried by the wind. Some studies estimate that tyre wear is among the largest sources of microplastics entering the environment.

LECTURER: In today's lecture, we're going to move away from the traditional economic model of the perfectly rational decision-maker and look at some insights from behavioural economics, focusing on a concept called loss aversion.
Traditional economic theory assumes that people evaluate outcomes in terms of their total wealth. Losing a hundred pounds and gaining a hundred pounds should therefore have equal and opposite effects. But in the 1970s, the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that this isn't how people actually behave. Their research, which contributed to Kahneman later receiving the Nobel Prize in economics, demonstrated that people evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point, usually their current situation, and that losses feel considerably more painful than equivalent gains feel pleasurable. Estimates vary, but many studies suggest losses weigh roughly twice as heavily.
A simple demonstration involves a coin toss. If people are offered a bet where they lose a hundred pounds on tails, most will refuse unless they stand to win around two hundred on heads, even though a smaller prize would still make the bet favourable.
Loss aversion helps explain several puzzling behaviours. One is the endowment effect. In a well-known experiment, some participants were given a mug and asked how much they would sell it for, while others were asked how much they would pay to buy one. Sellers typically demanded about twice as much as buyers were willing to pay. Simply owning the mug made it feel more valuable, because giving it up was experienced as a loss.
Another is the tendency to stick with the default option, sometimes called status quo bias. Changing from the default feels risky, because any potential losses loom larger than potential gains.
Governments and organisations have used these insights in policy design. A prominent example is pensions. In the UK, employers have been required since 2012 to enrol workers automatically in a pension scheme, although workers can choose to opt out. Participation rose sharply, not because people's preferences changed, but because the default changed.
However, I should add a note of caution. In recent years, some researchers have questioned how universal loss aversion really is. For small amounts of money, the effect is sometimes weak or absent, and it may depend on context. So while it's a powerful idea, it shouldn't be treated as a law of human behaviour.

LECTURER: Today we're turning to an animal that has become a central example in discussions of animal intelligence: the octopus.
Octopuses are molluscs, so their closest relatives include snails and clams. That makes their intelligence particularly interesting. The last common ancestor of octopuses and humans lived over five hundred million years ago and was probably a simple worm-like creature. This means that complex intelligence in octopuses evolved entirely independently from that in mammals and birds. Studying them may therefore tell us which features are necessary for intelligence and which are just accidents of our own evolutionary history.
Let's consider the nervous system. A common octopus has around five hundred million neurons, comparable to some mammals such as dogs. But the distribution is very unusual. Roughly two-thirds of these neurons are located not in the brain but in the arms. Each arm can carry out complex movements, and even respond to touch and taste, with considerable independence. Experiments have shown that an arm separated from the body can still reach for and grasp food.
What evidence is there of intelligence? Octopuses can solve problems such as opening screw-top jars to reach food. In laboratories, they've been observed escaping from tanks, and some individuals seem to recognise particular human keepers, behaving differently towards people they don't like. In the wild, one species has been filmed carrying coconut shells to use later as a shelter, which some researchers regard as a form of tool use.
Octopuses are also masters of camouflage. Their skin contains thousands of cells called chromatophores, each filled with pigment and controlled by muscles, allowing the animal to change colour within a fraction of a second. Some species can also change the texture of their skin to resemble rock or seaweed. Remarkably, octopuses appear to be colour-blind, and scientists are still investigating how they manage to match their surroundings so accurately.
Perhaps the greatest puzzle is their lifespan. Most octopuses live only one or two years. In most intelligent animals, a long life allows time for learning, often from parents. Octopuses, however, receive no parental care: the mother usually dies shortly after her eggs hatch. So whatever they know, they must learn by themselves, and quickly.
Finally, this research has had ethical consequences. In the UK, octopuses are now recognised as sentient beings in law, which affects how they may be treated.
